title: The autumn equinox
hookLine: balance again, and the light begins to shorten

lines: THE SAME BALANCE, FACING THE OTHER WAY.
cards: It shows up first at dinner. In August, dinner was eaten in daylight. Now the kitchen light is on before the pasta's done.
The mornings are cooler. The trees on your street have a few yellow leaves, like the first gray hairs. Back in the spring, the porch stood at the equinox and watched the light begin to win.
Today the scale balances again, day and night nearly even. But this time, in the north, the dark grows. The autumn equinox: the same balance, facing the other way.

teach.b: First, the turn. Astronomically, it's the mirror of spring: the sun crosses the equator heading south, and northern days grow shorter than the nights.
Some people feel it in their mood, a slight heaviness as evenings close in. That's real, and it's worth being gentle with. Second, Seneca in autumn.
In his twelfth letter, he visits his country house and grumbles to the caretaker that the old plane trees look neglected. The caretaker says he's doing all he can; the trees are just old.

Then Seneca remembers: he planted them himself. The trees are simply his age. And the letter turns: we should welcome and love old age, he says, because it is full of pleasure if you know how to use it.
Fruit is most welcome when it's almost over.
Third, turnings. For Seneca and Marcus, nature's cycles aren't something going wrong. Seasons turn, people age, the light comes and goes, and all of it belongs to the same whole.
You don't have to like the shorter days. You can stop treating them as a mistake. Fourth, what autumn offers.
The best light of the year, some say: low, gold, long shadows. Harvest. A slower pace.

teach.h: A DIFFERENT DAY, WITH ITS OWN GIFTS.
teach.b: It's a different kind of day with its own gifts, the way the later part of a life has its own.
Dusk shows it plainly, when day and night meet in the same sky.

how: Many cultures hold harvest festivals around the autumn equinox; some readers of the Stoics mark it with a dusk walk and a reflection on the seasons of life.

o: day and night even again, as the dark begins to grow
the year's last warm day, before winter sets in
the night the sun sets earliest of all the year

p: day and night in the same sky

s: Seneca blamed his caretaker for the old trees, and was right
the caretaker said the trees were just old, and Seneca realized he'd planted them himself.
Seneca writes that old age is full of pleasure if you know how to use it
after the autumn equinox, northern nights grow longer than days
the sun has crossed the equator heading south.

games.q: you're Seneca, scolding your caretaker about neglected old trees. he says they're just old. what do you do?
games.why: Seneca sees that he's as old as the trees, and turns the letter into praise of old age.

practice: Watch the light go from a window or a doorway, or picture a dusk you remember: the colors draining from the sky, the sounds changing, the air cooling. Don't hurry it, and don't hold on to it.
If a feeling of loss comes, let it be there; if rest comes, let that be there too.

wordCard.voice: Autumn equinox, when day and night return to balance but the light begins to shorten, a turning with its own gifts. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the turning. Not a mistake, just the other face of the year. See you tomorrow.
